title: meguri
status_note: Lab piece. The pipeline runs end to end on one card, but the series is pre-production: stills, storyboards and short test clips, no finished episode.
oneliner: A spring town in 3D, then riso anime shots from gray-box previz, on one GPU.
role: I built the local pipeline and am developing the original series Meguri with it: the Blender world and previz scenes, the ComfyUI and video workflows, the storyboards and the character looks.

body: I can block a shot as gray boxes in Blender and get an anime frame back that keeps the same camera, stairs and figure placement. The first panel is one shot, SH050 crane down the stair street, as four stages of one clock: the Blender previz, the depth and line passes, the ComfyUI job, and the finished clip.

The pipeline is Blender previz, then ComfyUI and a video model steered by depth passes, all on one 12 GB RTX 3060. Nothing is allowed to need more than 12 GB of VRAM, so I lean on 8-bit weights and tiled decode. Every generation is appended to a run log.

Meguri is an original series about a terraced spring town whose water runs downhill and still comes back to the top. The town is built as a 3D world from a plan, a map with 20 numbered camera positions, so every shot starts from a real place. I storyboard in previz first and spend GPU time on video only once a board is approved. The look is a two-ink riso print, one ink pair per character and place, and the geometry survives a change of print style.

What exists: stills, thirty-thumbnail storyboards, character turnarounds, and test clips of single shots such as the stair climb and the stair street. No episode is finished. What I learned: depth is the operator. Once the previz carries the camera and layout, the style becomes a setting I can change, and most failures are the model ignoring the scene rather than the scene being wrong. Character consistency and shot-to-shot continuity are not solved.

body: SHUTO is an action show about night couriers and rival bike gangs on an abandoned elevated expressway, where every on-ramp belongs to a gang and fights are blades at speed, with light trails. The first panel is one shot, SH13 the duel, as four stages of one clock: the Blender previz, a look-lab key, the video-model job, and the finished clip.

It runs on the same pipeline as Meguri on one 12 GB RTX 3060: a Blender previz scene with the choreography scripted, then depth-guided ComfyUI video. The expressway has its own 3D kit and a choreography tool; thirteen shots are blocked as previz, including the junction dive, the joust, the tunnel and the toll plaza, so the camera and the two bikes are fixed before any model touches them.

The look is the open question, so I run a look lab: fifteen looks across twelve frames each. Image models keep the layout but add riders, flip views and will not draw a head-on crossing, which is why the jousts come from previz, not from prompts. A blade and trail pass is added to the previz so the blades and the light trails follow the bikes.

What exists: previz clips for thirteen shots, 180 look-lab frames, a few finished test clips, and riso look plates for the cast. There is no finished episode and no chosen look yet. SURI, the sister idea from the same session, is shelved and not shown here.

title: tasty_tunez
status_note: Works locally on my GPU; the source is private for now while I decide how to release it.
oneliner: Songs from a text brief on your own GPU, each with a cover drawn from its notes.
role: I took a song apart to see what made it work, compared the open models and their licences, ran the experiments, and designed the app, the cover plates and the site. A Claude subagent built most of the app from my brief.

body: tasty_tunez turns a written brief into a two-minute song in about 20 seconds on a 12 GB card, using ACE-Step 1.5 (MIT). Every song comes out as an MP3 with its own cover plate and settings embedded, so it can be regenerated or remixed later.

It started with one slowed phonk track I liked. I measured it (tempo, key, stems, how dark and how bass-heavy) and then tested what moves a model toward that sound. The XL model and briefs written as sentences moved it; a community phonk LoRA moved it the other way. Those measurements became a feature: drop in a reference and the app suggests settings from fixed rules, each with the number behind it.
The model manager shows each model's licence before it downloads. YuE2 and LeVo 2 score well but are non-commercial or academic only, so the app lists them and explains why it doesn't install them.
What I learned: my reference song was about 7 dB louder than anything the model produced. Some of what makes a track hit is mastering, not generation.
